title: Many school supplies cost more under Trump's tariffs
gist: Using USITC DataWeb collections-over-CIF ratios, PIIE finds effective US tariff rates on six back-to-school goods categories rose 6 to 13 percentage points between H1 2024 and H1 2026 — backpacks now clear customs at a 27.8% effective rate — costing $5.33 billion in H1 2026 alone, an annualized $10.65 billion or roughly $79 per US household. The buried detail is asymmetry: clothing and footwear account for ~97% of the total burden, while tablets and laptops saw their effective tariff rate fall to 0.1% even as their import value tripled to $195.7 billion, producing a $218 million cost credit that is netted into the headline figure.

themes.theme: Effective tariff rates, measured from actual collections

insights.claim: Effective US tariff rates measured as customs revenue divided by CIF import value rose between 6 and 13 percentage points across six back-to-school product categories from the first half of 2024 to the first half of 2026.
insights.speaker: Gary Clyde Hufbauer,Ye Zhang
insights.so_what: Collections-over-CIF is the only tariff measure that captures exemptions, de minimis leakage and product-mix shifts — use it, not statutory schedules, when modelling COGS for import-dependent consumer names.
insights.quote: Tariff revenue rose by 6 to 13 percentage points in each of six different school-related categories, but it barely changed for tablets and laptops.
insights.locator: The table below shows the change

insights.claim: School backpacks (HS 420292) carry the highest effective US tariff rate in the sample, rising from 15.0% of CIF import value in H1 2024 to 27.8% in H1 2026, a 12.8 percentage-point increase.
insights.speaker: Gary Clyde Hufbauer,Ye Zhang
insights.so_what: A near-28% landed-cost tax on a low-ticket, price-elastic import is a direct gross-margin hit for discount and back-to-school retailers with no domestic substitute to shift toward.
insights.locator: Tariff revenue from these goods increased the most

insights.claim: Footwear's effective tariff rate roughly doubled from 11.6% to 22.5% of CIF import value between H1 2024 and H1 2026, adding $1.47 billion of import cost in the first half of 2026 alone.
insights.speaker: Gary Clyde Hufbauer,Ye Zhang
insights.so_what: Footwear (HS 64) already started from a high tariff base, so the increment stacks on top — margin compression here is arithmetically larger than in categories starting near zero.

insights.claim: Calculators saw the largest proportional jump in effective tariff rate — from 2.7% to 13.1% of CIF value, nearly a fivefold increase — but off a trivial import base of roughly $59 million per half-year.
insights.speaker: Gary Clyde Hufbauer,Ye Zhang
insights.so_what: A reminder that headline percentage-point moves and dollar impact diverge sharply by category; screen for import-value weight, not rate change, when sizing exposure.

insights.claim: Clothing (HS 61-62) went from a 13.8% to a 23.8% effective tariff rate, and notebooks and pencils/pens moved from roughly 6% to 12.3% and 14.3% respectively.
insights.speaker: Gary Clyde Hufbauer,Ye Zhang
insights.so_what: Effective rates in the low-20s on apparel are a structural, not cyclical, input-cost shift for the entire soft-goods retail complex.

insights.claim: The analysis directly contradicts White House claims and concludes that tariffs raise the price of landed imports, meaning tariffs on school supplies are paid by American households and businesses rather than by foreign exporters.
insights.speaker: Gary Clyde Hufbauer,Ye Zhang
insights.so_what: If the incidence sits domestically, tariffs function as a consumption tax with a delayed CPI signature — a reason to expect goods disinflation to stall rather than resume.
insights.quote: Contrary to White House claims(link is external), the analysis shows that tariffs result in higher prices of landed imports
insights.locator: The figure below portrays the table data

insights.claim: Importing firms that pay the tariffs choose how much to pass through, with some raising prices by less and some by more than the tariff cost, so the landed-cost increase is not a one-to-one predictor of shelf prices.
insights.speaker: Gary Clyde Hufbauer,Ye Zhang
insights.so_what: The split between margin absorption and consumer pass-through is the single variable determining whether tariffs show up in retailer earnings or in CPI — track gross margins alongside price indices, not either alone.
insights.quote: Some firms raise prices by less or by more than the cost of the tariffs.
insights.locator: Importing firms that pay the tariffs

insights.claim: The United States depends heavily on imports for basic low-cost products like backpacks, notebooks, pencils, calculators and footwear, leaving little domestic substitution capacity to blunt tariff incidence.
insights.speaker: Gary Clyde Hufbauer,Ye Zhang
insights.so_what: Absent a domestic supply response, tariffs on these SKUs are close to pure price effects — the reshoring thesis has no near-term expression in this product set.
insights.quote: The United States depends heavily on imports for these basic low-cost products.

themes.theme: The laptop exemption hiding in the data

insights.claim: Tablets and laptops (HS 8471) saw their effective tariff rate fall from 0.3% to 0.1% of CIF import value between H1 2024 and H1 2026 — the only category in the sample where the tariff burden declined.
insights.speaker: Gary Clyde Hufbauer,Ye Zhang
insights.so_what: Computing hardware was effectively carved out of the tariff regime while low-value consumer goods were not — a regressive split that argues for underweighting soft-goods importers relative to hardware channel names.

insights.claim: CIF import value for tablets and laptops more than tripled from $61.2 billion in the first half of 2024 to $195.7 billion in the first half of 2026, dwarfing every other category in the dataset.
insights.speaker: Gary Clyde Hufbauer,Ye Zhang
insights.so_what: A $134 billion half-year jump in automatic data-processing machine imports, arriving tariff-free, is a large and under-discussed import-side signal worth reconciling against the compute-buildout narrative and the goods trade deficit.

insights.claim: Because the tablets/laptops effective rate fell, the category generates a negative $218.17 million cost figure that is netted into the headline aggregate, meaning the gross tariff cost across the six burdened categories is roughly $5.54 billion rather than the reported $5.33 billion.
insights.speaker: Gary Clyde Hufbauer,Ye Zhang
insights.so_what: The headline per-household number understates the burden on households that do not buy a laptop — the offset is concentrated in a category most back-to-school shoppers do not purchase annually.
insights.locator: The combined cost of Trump's increased tariffs

insights.claim: The combined increased tariff cost across the listed product categories was $5.33 billion for the first half of 2026, implying a full-year total of $10.65 billion at the same run rate.
insights.speaker: Gary Clyde Hufbauer,Ye Zhang
insights.so_what: A ~$10.7 billion annual figure from a narrow slice of consumer goods sets a scaling benchmark for extrapolating the total consumer tariff burden across all import categories.
insights.locator: The combined cost of Trump's increased tariffs

insights.claim: Clothing and footwear alone account for $3.68 billion and $1.47 billion of the H1 2026 increased import cost — roughly 97% of the gross burden — while notebooks, pencils, calculators and backpacks together contribute under $400 million.
insights.speaker: Gary Clyde Hufbauer,Ye Zhang
insights.so_what: The 'school supplies' framing is really an apparel and footwear story; exposure screening should center on soft-goods sourcing, not stationery.

insights.claim: Annual tariff costs for the affected back-to-school goods are projected to average $79 higher per US household in 2026 than in 2024, derived by dividing the $10.65 billion annualized cost across approximately 135 million US households.
insights.speaker: Gary Clyde Hufbauer,Ye Zhang
insights.so_what: A quantified per-household hit on non-discretionary basics gives a floor estimate for the real-income drag feeding into low-income consumer spending and discount-retail traffic.
insights.quote: fifth grade arithmetic indicates that the average annual cost per household would be about $79 higher this year than in 2024
insights.locator: Since US households number approximately 135 million

insights.claim: Nominal CIF import values fell between H1 2024 and H1 2026 for clothing ($38.1bn to $37.0bn), notebooks ($548m to $500m), pencils and pens ($821m to $740m) and school backpacks ($2,302m to $2,277m), while footwear was roughly flat.
insights.speaker: Gary Clyde Hufbauer,Ye Zhang
insights.so_what: Declining nominal import values across two years of inflation imply real volume compression in tariffed consumer goods — a demand-destruction signal that also mechanically shrinks the estimated cost base.

insights.claim: The cost estimate is constructed as H1 2026 total CIF import value multiplied by the change in the tariff revenue ratio between H1 2024 and H1 2026, a method that measures the increase in landed cost rather than the increase in retail prices.
insights.speaker: Gary Clyde Hufbauer,Ye Zhang
insights.so_what: Reusable methodology: any HS code plus USITC DataWeb collections data yields a comparable effective-tariff and cost-delta estimate for other consumer categories.

insights.claim: The affected products were hit with higher tariffs across six categories since Donald Trump returned to the presidency in early 2025, making the 2024-to-2026 comparison a clean before-and-after of a single policy regime change.
insights.speaker: Gary Clyde Hufbauer,Ye Zhang
insights.so_what: The tariff step-change is recent and fully in the run rate only from 2025 onward, so year-over-year comparisons through 2026 will keep showing base effects that fade in 2027.
